processing: Grown mainly for shaded tea: the bushes are covered before picking and the leaf is steamed and dried as tencha, then stone-milled into matcha, or finished as gyokuro.
harvest_season: Spring first flush, shaded before picking, with the first picking most prized for matcha.
appearance_dry: As matcha, a fine, vivid green powder.
appearance_liquor: Opaque bright green when whisked, with a fine froth.
appearance_wet: Whisked matcha leaves no whole leaf; as tencha or gyokuro the shaded leaf is soft and deep green.
taste_profile: Sweet and rich in umami with little bitterness, often described with a light citrus lift.

brewing.notes: Sift the powder, add water below boiling and whisk until frothy. Too much heat flattens the sweetness.

vintage_note: Sold by cultivar and maker rather than by vintage, as single-cultivar matcha or in blends, usually from the most recent spring harvest. Once opened, matcha loses aroma and colour fast, so buy small tins and check the packing date.
description:
Samidori is one of the old cultivars behind Uji matcha, and the name drinkers look for when they want to taste that classic Kyoto style unblended. It is widely described as the leading tencha cultivar in Kyoto, and the prefecture counts it among its Uji cultivars. Do not confuse it with Saemidori, a different and separately bred tea.

It was selected for shaded production, and its upright-growing leaves suit hand picking. Most of it becomes tencha and then matcha, though it also appears in gyokuro. It is not an easy crop; one producer notes a low yield.

In the bowl it is sweet and full of umami, usually with a touch of citrus and not much bitterness. Whisk it with water below boiling; a thick koicha-style preparation shows off that body, but a normal thin bowl is a good place to begin.

Single-cultivar Samidori is sold by makers in Uji, Wazuka and Shirakawa, and small amounts are grown outside Kyoto, including in Yame. Many Uji matchas blend it with others, so look for the cultivar name on the tin if you want it alone. Comparing it side by side with an Asahi matcha is an easy lesson in what cultivar does.
history:
Samidori is credited to the Uji breeder Masajiro Koyama (小山政次郎). It was selected from his garden in Kyoto Prefecture in the early Showa period, with 1939 the date usually given, from native Uji stock.

Accounts differ on its later status: several describe it as technically unregistered, while another lists a 1953 registration. One gives 1954 as the year its planting began to be encouraged. Today Kyoto Prefecture supports planting it as an Uji cultivar.
